title: Equilibria
overview: Work with Ka, Kw and pH for acids and bases, understand how buffers resist pH change, and use Ksp and partition coefficients. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Use Ka, pKa, Kw and pH for strong and weak acids/bases.
Explain and calculate buffer action and buffer pH.
Use Ksp to calculate solubility and predict precipitation.
Use partition coefficients for solute distribution between immiscible solvents.

definitions.definition: A solution that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.
Ksp, the equilibrium constant for dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid.
The equilibrium concentration ratio of a solute between two immiscible solvents at a fixed temperature.

sections.title: Acid–base equilibria
content: For weak HA, Ka=[H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] and pKa=−log₁₀Ka. Set up an equilibrium table and use approximations only when justified. Kw=[H⁺][OH⁻]=1.00×10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K, so pH+pOH=14 at that temperature.
bullets: Strong describes extent of ionisation, not concentration.
Check any small-x approximation against the initial concentration.

sections.title: Buffers
content: An acidic buffer contains HA and A⁻. Added H⁺ is removed by A⁻; added OH⁻ is removed by HA. Use [H⁺]=Ka[HA]/[A⁻] or pH=pKa+log([A⁻]/[HA]), after accounting stoichiometrically for any added strong acid/base.
bullets: Use mole ratios when both components share the same final volume.
Buffer capacity is finite and greatest when both components are substantial.

sections.title: Ksp and precipitation
content: Write the dissolution equation before the Ksp expression. For MX₂⇌M²⁺+2X⁻, Ksp=[M²⁺][X⁻]²; molar solubility s gives s(2s)². After mixing solutions, calculate diluted ion concentrations and compare ionic product Qsp with Ksp.
bullets: Stoichiometric coefficients become powers and concentration multipliers.

sections.title: Partition and extraction
content: For solute X, Kpc=[X]organic/[X]aqueous using the stated order. Calculate amount remaining from equilibrium concentration ratios and phase volumes. Several small extractions remove more solute than one extraction with the same total solvent volume.
bullets: Use concentrations, not raw moles, in Kpc.
The solute must have the same molecular form in both solvents unless the question accounts for reaction.

formulas.label: Partition
formulas.note: Use the order defined in the question.

examTips: Write an equilibrium equation before every constant expression.
For buffer additions, do stoichiometric neutralisation before the equilibrium calculation.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Putting solids or liquid water into equilibrium expressions.
Ignoring dilution after mixing solutions for Ksp.
Using initial buffer amounts after strong acid/base has reacted.

quickRecall.question: How does an acidic buffer remove added H⁺?
quickRecall.answer: Its conjugate base A⁻ reacts with H⁺ to form HA.

quickRecall.question: When does precipitation begin?
quickRecall.answer: When the ionic product reaches Ksp; Qsp>Ksp favours solid formation.

quickRecall.question: Why are several extractions more effective?
quickRecall.answer: Each fresh portion establishes a new partition equilibrium and removes a fraction of what remains.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between strong and concentrated?
quickRecall.answer: Strong means nearly complete ionisation; concentrated means many moles per unit volume.
